title: Searching the recursion tree improves the lower bound on the Shannon capacity of C7
description:
A lower bound Θ(C7) ≥ 3.258834362237710794…, improving 3.258832620353266309… (Tandon, arXiv:2608.30273), obtained from published data alone.

The recent sequence of improvements to this bound shares a common shape: a library of admissible combining rules is applied along a fixed recursion tree. The rules have been studied carefully; the tree has not. Optimising the tree gives the improvement. The construction is the Buys–Polak–Zuiddam terminal code K4a applied to four copies of S3b(n6, n11, n11), where n6 and n11 are Tandon's own published cardinality vectors; the only change from the published construction is that the third input is a second copy of n11 rather than n8, so the ordered split 25 = 6 + 11 + 8 becomes 28 = 6 + 11 + 11 and the dimension grows from 500 to 560. Among all 16384 combinations of the three published blocks the published choice is third by value.

The deposit contains the certificate (a seven-family cardinality vector in C7⊠140 and the resulting 288-digit independent set in C7⊠560), two dependency-free verifiers sharing no code and taking their copies of the rules from different sources (Node.js from the Lean sources of the BPZ repository, Python from the printed tables), the exhaustive search over combinations, and the census and obstruction checks behind the negative results.

The note also records what does not help, since several natural avenues can be closed exhaustively rather than merely explored: the Polak–Schrijver base gadget admits exactly eight private pairs and this is a structural ceiling; its neutral auxiliary part cannot exceed 322 over the entire automorphism orbit; bases with nine and even ten private pairs exist but are incompatible with a full-sized auxiliary set, the doubly covered region growing by about 142 forbidden vertices per additional pair; and the published twist is optimal over all 64538880 automorphisms. Two traps that internal consistency does not catch are described.

The search over recursion trees, the exhaustive verifications and both implementations were carried out with the assistance of a large language model. All results are reproducible from the scripts and certificates supplied; the Python verification was written independently of the search code and from the printed rule tables rather than from the machine-readable sources, so that it does not share the assumptions of the code that produced the result. Each verifier reproduces the published construction as a control before evaluating the new one.
